notes.meaning: Job begins his reply to Zophar and the other companions. Instead of focusing only on his own grief, he turns to examine their claims about how God runs the world.
Job asks his friends to give him their full attention. If they have no helpful words to share, simply listening with patience will be the comfort he desires from them.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The ancient Greek translation turns this sentence into a negative statement, suggesting the friends offered no true comfort.

notes.meaning: Job asks his companions to let him speak without cutting him off. After he finishes explaining his case, they can continue mocking him if they still wish.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The Hebrew command to mock is singular, which may mean Job addresses Zophar alone because Zophar spoke last.

notes.meaning: Job explains that his deep struggle is with God, not with mortal human beings. Because God remains silent and seems to treat him as guilty, it is natural for him to feel restless and impatient.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Job may be pointing out that while human disputes can find sympathetic listeners, no one dares to show sympathy to someone who questions God.

notes.meaning: Job invites his friends to look directly at his shattered condition and be stunned. Placing a hand over the mouth was an ancient custom showing humble, awe-filled silence before an unsolved mystery.
Job admits that simply thinking about his sudden ruin fills him with dread. The fact that a righteous person can lose everything while evil people prosper makes his entire body shake with fear.
Job directly challenges the idea that evil people are always cut down quickly. Daily experience shows that many wicked people live long lives, reach old age, and grow steadily in power and wealth.
The friends had insisted that the wicked leave no family behind. Job points out that evil people often see their children and grandchildren grow up safe, healthy, and firmly established.
Many wicked households enjoy lasting safety and are free from sudden terror. God does not seem to strike them with His rod of discipline or bring ruin upon their properties.
Job describes the thriving business and farming success of the wicked. Their cattle breed successfully, and their herds produce healthy calves without barrenness or miscarriages.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Rabbinic tradition and modern translation notes understand the Hebrew phrasing to mean the breeding bull does not fail to do its work.

notes.meaning: The children of these wicked households run outside to play like healthy young lambs in a pasture. They sing and dance happily to the music of tambourines, harps, and flutes.
These ungodly people spend their days enjoying prosperity and ease. Instead of suffering through long, painful illnesses like Job, they die quickly and peacefully.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The Hebrew term can mean either in a moment or in peace, picturing a quiet passing with no lingering agony.

notes.meaning: Despite enjoying every earthly advantage, these prospering people tell God to leave them alone. Their rebellious actions show that they have no interest in learning His commands or walking in His ways.
The wicked proudly ask what obligation they have to worship the Almighty. They measure life only by selfish worldly advantage and see no practical profit in offering prayer to God.

Job recognizes that the wealth of the wicked is not something they created or control by their own power, since all blessings come from God. Even though sinners thrive, Job completely rejects their godless way of life and wants no part in their thinking.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Traditional Catholic translations read the second half of this sentence as a prayer, asking God to keep the advice of the wicked far away.

notes.meaning: Job asks how often the lamp of the wicked is really snuffed out as his friends claim. In actual life, God rarely seems to send immediate, overwhelming disaster upon notorious sinners.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The word for sorrows can refer to sudden birth pangs or binding cords, picturing severe distress that rarely falls on the prosperous wicked.

notes.meaning: Job continues his question, asking how often the ungodly are actually blown away like straw or chaff in a gale. They often stay rooted and comfortable rather than being swept away by sudden judgment.
The friends argued that God saves up a sinner's punishment for his children. Job replies that justice should fall upon the guilty man himself so that he personally feels the consequence of his evil.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Translators often add the words they say at the beginning to show Job is quoting a common argument from his companions.

notes.meaning: Job urges that the wicked man should see his own downfall with his own eyes while he is still alive. The wrongdoer himself ought to drink the bitter cup of the Almighty's wrath.

Once a wicked person dies and his life is over, he does not care about what happens to the family he leaves behind. Punishing his descendants after he is gone does not bring correction to the sinner himself.
Job asks whether any human being can pretend to instruct God in how to govern creation. God is the supreme Judge who rules over all things, including the highest rulers and heavenly beings.
One person dies while still strong, robust, and completely free from worry. His body is well-nourished, and his bones remain moist and healthy right up to the end of his days.

Another person dies after a life filled with bitter grief, having never experienced good health, wealth, or happiness. God distributes earthly circumstances in varied ways that humans cannot predict or fully explain.
In the end, death places both the prosperous and the afflicted on the very same level. Both lie down in the dust of the grave, and worms cover them without showing any favoritism.
Job tells his friends that he knows their inner thoughts and silent conclusions. He recognizes their quiet scheme to use his severe misery as proof that he must be a secret sinner.

The friends had repeatedly asked what becomes of the houses of ruthless rulers and tyrants. By pointing out that the dwellings of wicked men fall into ruins, they were hinting that the destruction of Job's house proved his guilt.
Job tells them to ask travelers who have journeyed far and seen the wider world. Anyone with broad life experience knows that the friends' simple rule about life does not fit real facts.
Job states that evil people are often spared from calamity during this earthly life. Their true reckoning is kept for the final day of judgment and wrath in the world to come.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars translate this verse to say the evil person is spared during disaster and safely escorted away when wrath breaks out in this life.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Traditional Catholic commentary notes that the wicked may either be kept safe during present calamities or reserved for the last day of punishment.

notes.meaning: While a tyrant lives in wealth and power, nobody dares to confront him to his face about his wicked deeds. Because people fear his power, no human court holds him accountable or forces him to repay what he stole.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Both questions in this verse are rhetorical, expecting the plain answer that no one dares to challenge such a powerful wrongdoer.

notes.meaning: When the wicked man finally dies, he is carried to his grave with great honor and ceremony. A grand monument is built over his resting place so that his memory is watched over and honored.

The dirt of the burial valley lies softly upon him, and huge crowds march in his funeral procession. In dying, he simply meets the universal end that countless people met before him and all will face after him.

Job concludes that his companions offer nothing but empty and misleading comfort. Their advice is useless because it rests on the false claim that good people always prosper and evil people always suffer in this present life.
